pages.content: # Welcome to YAGSL Brought to you by Yet Another Generic Swerve Library (YAGSL) {% hint style="warning" %} If your swerve drive uses only [Falcon500](https://store.ctr-electronics.com/falcon-500-powered-by-talon-fx/)/[Kraken](https://store.ctr-electronics.com/kraken-x60/)/[TalonFXS](https://store.ctr-electronics.com/products/talon-fxs), [Pigeon2.0](https://store.ctr-electronics.com/pigeon-2/), and [CANCoder](https://store.ctr-electronics.com/cancoder/) from [CTRE](https://pro.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/latest/index.html) please also consider the [Tuner X Swerve Drive Generator](https://pro.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/latest/docs/tuner/tuner-swerve/index.html). {% endhint %} ## Overview YAGSL is a Swerve Library developed by current and former BroncBotz mentors for all FRC teams. YAGSL is a JSON configuration parser that builds a [YAMS](https://yams.yamgen.com/) `SwerveDrive` for your robot: describe your hardware once, generate the config at [**config.yagsl.com**](https://config.yagsl.com), and drive. See [What is YAGSL?](/explanation/what-is-yagsl.md) for how the pieces fit together. {% hint style="success" %} YAGSL 2027 is built on WPILib 2027 (`2027_alpha7`, Java 25) and runs on the SystemCore. It supports both WPILib Commands v2 and Commands v3, each with its own vendordep. See the [Changelog](/explanation/changelog.md) for what changed in the 2027 port. {% endhint %} {% embed url="" %} ## This documentation is organized into four sections * [**Tutorial**](/tutorial/tutorial.md): never used YAGSL before? Start here. A single linear walkthrough from a bare WPILib project to a driving swerve robot. * [**How-to Guides**](/how-to-guides/how-to.md): already have a robot running? Task-focused recipes for tuning PIDF, determining inversion, diagnosing drift, and other work you'll come back to. * [**Reference**](/reference/reference.md): precise JSON schema field tables, supported hardware type strings, and where to find the YAMS API docs. * [**Explanation**](/explanation/explanation.md): swerve drive theory and the reasoning behind how YAGSL and YAMS behave. {% hint style="info" %} Upgrading an existing robot from before **2026.8.05**? Your `swerve/` config directory uses the old schema. See [Schema Changes](/reference/schema-changes.md) before you do anything else. {% endhint %} ## Get started The quickest way to spin up YAGSL is the [config generator](https://config.yagsl.com) and its **Quick Start Guide**. Fill in the generator's form, press **Download Config**, and the Quick Start Guide walks you through the rest, one checklist at a time: copy the YAGSL example project, drop your config into it, tune it in simulation, then calibrate and tune the real robot. The generator works on a phone too, and its **Print** button prints the whole form, so you can fill it in on paper at the robot and type it in later. The [tutorial](/tutorial/tutorial.md) covers the same ground in more detail, including adding YAGSL to a project you already have. {% embed url="" %} {% content-ref url="/pages/VUjPRU3oP9Kpxefm9ap7" %} [Your First Swerve Robot](/tutorial/tutorial.md) {% endcontent-ref %} {% content-ref url="/pages/QcM0FunHvaMONGWx5YYK" %} [Tune PIDF gains](/how-to-guides/tune-pidf-gains.md) {% endcontent-ref %} {% content-ref url="/pages/VLPyZoQy6yIAwWwW5pmV" %} [The 8 steps](/how-to-guides/the-8-steps.md) {% endcontent-ref %} {% content-ref url="/pages/kLO6AjaFJTb3Q1dvCozW" %} [Schema Changes (Migrating to 2027 and from pre-2026.8.05)](/reference/schema-changes.md) {% endcontent-ref %} ## YAGSL Online Installation Install **exactly one** of these vendordeps, matching the WPILib command framework your robot uses (they conflict with each other): | Command framework | Vendordep URL | | ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | | Commands v2 | `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/yagsl_commands2.json` | | Commands v3 | `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/yagsl_commands3.json` | Each one requires only the matching [YAMS](https://yams.yamgen.com/) vendordep (`https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/yams_commands2.json` or `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/yams_commands3.json`). Vendor libraries such as REVLib, Phoenix 6, ReduxLib and ThriftyLib are only needed for the hardware your robot actually has. See [Install YAGSL](/tutorial/02-install-yagsl.md) for the full steps, including the offline install. {% hint style="warning" %} The old `https://yet-another-software-suite.github.io/YAGSL/...` vendordep and maven URLs are stale. Remove the old `yagsl.json` from your `vendordeps` folder and install one of the URLs above. {% endhint %} ## Our Philosophy Your program does not revolve around your swerve drive. Your constants file doesn't have to take 10 minutes to find the right option. Different robots should be able to work with the same code: swap the `swerve/` config directory and the same subsystem code drives a different robot. --- # Agent Instructions This documentation is published with GitBook. pages.title: Your First Swerve Robot
pages.content:
# Your First Swerve Robot

This tutorial takes a team from a bare WPILib project to a driving swerve robot using YAGSL. Follow the five steps in order. Each one builds on the last, and by the end your robot will be driving under field-relative control with a tuned configuration.

{% hint style="success" %}
**The quickest path is the config generator's Quick Start Guide.** Fill in the form at [config.yagsl.com](https://config.yagsl.com) and press **Download Config**: the Quick Start Guide opens with checklists that take you from the YAGSL example project to a tuned robot. This tutorial explains the same steps in more depth, and how to add YAGSL to a project you already have.
{% endhint %}

{% hint style="warning" %}
Swerve drives are complicated and will not "just work" on the first try. If you've never brought up a swerve drive before, budget more than one sitting for this because gathering accurate information about your robot and calibrating hardware always takes longer than expected. If you've done this before, expect this tutorial to take about 30 minutes plus PID tuning time.
{% endhint %}

## Prerequisites

* WPILib 2027 (`2027_alpha7`) installed, and a WPILib Java robot project (new or existing) that uses either Commands v2 or Commands v3. YAGSL supports both, see [Install YAGSL](/tutorial/02-install-yagsl.md).
* A SystemCore robot controller.
* Your swerve modules are physically assembled and wired (motors, absolute encoders, gyroscope all on the robot).
* You know how to deploy code to your robot and open a driver dashboard (Shuffleboard, Elastic, or AdvantageScope).

{% hint style="info" %}
If your swerve drive uses only [Falcon500](https://store.ctr-electronics.com/falcon-500-powered-by-talon-fx/)/[Kraken](https://store.ctr-electronics.com/kraken-x60/)/[TalonFXS](https://store.ctr-electronics.com/products/talon-fxs), [Pigeon2.0](https://store.ctr-electronics.com/pigeon-2/), and [CANCoder](https://store.ctr-electronics.com/cancoder/) from CTRE, you can also consider the [Tuner X Swerve Drive Generator](https://pro.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/latest/docs/tuner/tuner-swerve/index.html) as an alternative. YAGSL supports a much wider range of hardware and mixes vendors freely.
{% endhint %}

## The five steps

1. [Gather your robot information](/tutorial/01-gather-your-robot-information.md): collect the CAN IDs, gear ratios, and module locations you'll need before you touch any software.
2. [Install YAGSL](/tutorial/02-install-yagsl.md): add the YAGSL vendordep for your command framework, the YAMS vendordep it requires, and the vendordeps for the hardware your robot has.
3. [Generate your configuration](/tutorial/03-generate-your-configuration.md): use [config.yagsl.com](https://config.yagsl.com) to turn your robot information into a config directory.
4. [Verify and calibrate your hardware](/tutorial/04-verify-and-calibrate-hardware.md): confirm every motor, encoder, and gyro reports direction correctly, and capture absolute encoder offsets.
5. [Deploy and drive](/tutorial/05-deploy-and-drive.md): wire up `SwerveParser` in a subsystem (Commands v2) or mechanism (Commands v3), bind your controller, and take your robot for its first drive.

Once you're driving, see the **How-to Guides** section for tuning PIDF gains, diagnosing drift, and other tasks you'll come back to as you keep developing.


---

pages.title: Gather your robot information
pages.content: # Gather your robot information {% hint style="info" %} Print the [config generator](https://config.yagsl.com) with its **Print** button and take it to the robot. Every tab prints on paper with the options listed and a blank line for each value, so you can fill it in as you gather this information and type it into the website later. {% endhint %} YAGSL is configured entirely from information about *your* robot. There is no universal constants file that works for everyone. Before opening [config.yagsl.com](https://config.yagsl.com), collect everything in this step. Having it all on hand up front saves you from re-measuring later. {% hint style="warning" %} Every swerve drive is different, even between robots using the same COTS modules (SDS MK4, MAXSwerve, etc.). Don't assume your numbers match another team's example. {% endhint %} ## Hardware types and connections | Feature | Notes | | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Gyroscope model and connection | e.g. Pigeon 2.0 on CAN, Canandgyro on CAN, NavX3 on CAN (not usable with YAGSL 2027 yet, because StudicaLib has no `2027_alpha7` build), or the IMU built into the SystemCore (no wiring or CAN ID needed). | | Drive motor + controller for each module | e.g. Kraken X60 on TalonFX, NEO on SparkMAX, NEO on a Thrifty Nova, etc. | | Angle/steering motor + controller for each module | Same as above, per module. | | Absolute encoder model and connection for each module | e.g. CANcoder on CAN, a REV Through Bore attached to the angle motor controller's data port, or an encoder wired to a SystemCore DIO or analog port (record the channel). | | CAN bus of every CAN device | The SystemCore has several CAN buses, so record which one each device is wired to: `can_s0` (bus `0`, the default) through `can_s4` (bus `4`). CTRE devices on a [CANivore](https://store.ctr-electronics.com/canivore/) use the CANivore's configured name instead. See the note below. | | CAN ID / channel of every motor controller, encoder, and gyro | Get this wrong and you'll be controlling the wrong device without realizing it. | {% hint style="info" %} Every device's `canbus` value is read the same way, whichever vendor made it: leave it empty for `can_s0`, or enter the bus number, `0` to `4` for `can_s0` to `can_s4` (so `1` is `can_s1`), and `5` to `24` for the Motioncore buses `can_d0` to `can_d19`. Only CTRE devices also accept a CANivore name. REV and Thrifty devices only accept a bus number. {% endhint %} ## Physical characteristics | Feature | Relevance | | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Drive gear ratio | How many drive motor rotations produce one wheel rotation. Usually published by the module manufacturer. | | Steering/angle gear ratio | How many steering motor rotations produce one full module rotation. Also published by the manufacturer. | | Wheel diameter | Needed to convert motor rotations into distance traveled. | | Module locations | Distance in inches from the robot's center to each module's center, split into "front" (X) and "left" (Y) components. See below for how to measure this. | ### Measuring module locations Measure in CAD if you can, for precision; otherwise, use this technique from Team 5010: 1. Lay the robot on its side and rotate the wheels perpendicular to the direction you're measuring. 2. Measure to the *outside* of each wheel and subtract one wheel width to get the center-to-center measurement. 3. Repeat in the other direction. Record all four module locations (front-left, front-right, back-left, back-right) relative to the robot's center, in inches: | Module | X "Front" (in) | Y "Left" (in) | | ---------------- | -------------- | ------------- | | Front Left (FL) | + | + | | Front Right (FR) | + | − | | Back Left (BL) | − | + | | Back Right (BR) | − | − | ## Inversion and offsets: record placeholders now, fill in later You won't be able to determine these until your code is deployed (that happens in [step 4](/tutorial/04-verify-and-calibrate-hardware.md)), but it helps to have a table ready: | Module | Drive Inverted? | Angle Inverted? | Absolute Encoder Inverted? | Absolute Encoder Offset (°) | | ---------------- | --------------- | --------------- | -------------------------- | --------------------------- | | Front Left (FL) | | | | | | Front Right (FR) | | | | | | Back Left (BL) | | | | | | Back Right (BR) | | | | | Also note whether your gyroscope needs to be inverted. It must report an **increasing** yaw while the robot rotates counterclockwise. {% hint style="info" %} A printable version of a bring-up checklist covering all of the above (courtesy of DevilBotz 2876) is available in the repository's asset folder if your team prefers a paper checklist during bring-up. {% endhint %} With this information in hand, move on to [installing YAGSL](/tutorial/02-install-yagsl.md). --- # Agent Instructions This documentation is published with GitBook. pages.title: Install YAGSL
pages.content: # Install YAGSL YAGSL 2027 is built on WPILib 2027 (`2027_alpha7`) and Java 25, and runs on the SystemCore. Install the matching WPILib release first, then create or open your robot project. ## Add the YAGSL vendordep YAGSL ships as two vendordeps, one per WPILib command framework. Install **exactly one** of them, the one that matches the command framework your robot project uses. They conflict with each other, so do not install both. | Command framework | Vendordep name | Vendordep URL | | ----------------- | ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | | Commands v2 | YAGSL (Commands v2) | `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/yagsl_commands2.json` | | Commands v3 | YAGSL (Commands v3) | `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/yagsl_commands3.json` | In VS Code, run **WPILib: Manage Vendor Libraries → Install new libraries (online)** and paste the URL for your command framework. {% hint style="info" %} Not sure which one to pick? Use Commands v2 if your project uses `SubsystemBase` and PathPlanner. Use Commands v3 if your project uses `Mechanism`s, coroutines and the OpMode framework. The rest of this tutorial shows both where they differ. {% endhint %} {% hint style="warning" %} Upgrading an older project? The old `https://yet-another-software-suite.github.io/YAGSL/...` vendordep and maven URLs are stale. Delete the old `yagsl.json` (and the old `yams.json`) from your project's `vendordeps` folder, then install the URLs on this page. YAGSL now resolves from `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/`. {% endhint %} ## Add the YAMS vendordep (required) YAGSL builds a [YAMS](https://yams.yamgen.com/) `SwerveDrive`, so the matching YAMS vendordep is the one library the YAGSL vendordep requires. VS Code offers to install it when you add YAGSL. If it does not, install it the same way: | Command framework | Vendordep URL | | ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | | Commands v2 | `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/yams_commands2.json` | | Commands v3 | `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/yams_commands3.json` | YAMS in turn requires the matching WPILib command framework vendordep (Commands v2 or Commands v3). ## Add vendordeps for your hardware (optional) YAGSL does not require any hardware vendor library. It only loads a vendor's classes when your JSON configuration uses one of that vendor's devices, so install a vendordep for the hardware your robot actually has and skip the rest: | Vendor | Needed for | | -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | CTRE Phoenix 6 | TalonFX, TalonFXS, Pigeon 2.0, CANcoder | | REVLib | SparkMAX, SparkFlex, REV spline encoder | | ReduxLib | Canandgyro, Canandmag | | ThriftyLib | Thrifty Nova | | Studica | NavX3 (no `2027_alpha7` build yet, see the warning below) | | None | SystemCore IMU, and encoders wired to the SystemCore's DIO or analog ports | Use the 2027 build of each vendor library. If your configuration names a device whose vendor library is not installed, the project still builds, but the robot program fails at startup when `SwerveParser` tries to create that device. {% hint style="warning" %} StudicaLib and the AndyMark library have not published a `2027_alpha7` vendordep yet. Until they do, the `navx3_can` gyro and the `andymarkhexbore_can` encoder cannot be used with YAGSL 2027. {% endhint %} {% hint style="info" %} If a vendor isn't in the Vendor Dependencies panel yet on your WPILib version, install it the manual way instead. [Installing 3rd-party libraries](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/2027/docs/software/vscode-overview/3rd-party-libraries.html) covers pasting a URL, which you can get from the vendor's own install page. {% endhint %} {% hint style="warning" %} Your vendor's hardware client (REV Hardware Client, Phoenix Tuner X) is a separate tool from the vendordep. Install it too, it's needed for firmware updates and low-level device configuration. {% endhint %} ## Offline install If your network blocks the download, get `-YAGSL-Offline.zip` from the [YAGSL GitHub releases](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAGSL/releases). It contains a `maven` folder and a `vendordeps` folder that merge into your WPILib `2027_alpha7` home folder: * **Windows:** extract into `C:\Users\Public\wpilib\2027_alpha7` * **macOS and Linux:** extract into `~/wpilib/2027_alpha7` Then run **WPILib: Manage Vendor Libraries → Install new libraries (offline)** and pick **YAGSL (Commands v2)** or **YAGSL (Commands v3)**. YAMS has a matching `-YAMS-Offline.zip` on its own [releases page](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/releases), installed the same way. Run a Gradle build afterward to pull down the libraries before continuing. Once your build succeeds with all vendordeps installed, move on to [generating your configuration](/tutorial/03-generate-your-configuration.md). --- # Agent Instructions This documentation is published with GitBook. pages.title: Generate your configuration
pages.content: # Generate your configuration Since 2026, the supported way to configure YAGSL is [config.yagsl.com](https://config.yagsl.com), a web app that builds your configuration files from a guided form instead of you hand-writing JSON. It runs entirely in your browser, and it produces the same files for Commands v2 and Commands v3 projects. * **On a phone:** the whole generator works on a phone, so you can fill it in at the robot. * **On paper:** **Print** prints every tab, with the dropdown options listed and a blank line for each value. Fill it in by hand, then type it in later. * **Quick Start Guide:** **Download Config** opens the generator's Quick Start Guide, a printable checklist that takes you from the YAGSL example project, through tuning in simulation, to calibrating and tuning the real robot. It is the quickest way to spin up YAGSL; the rest of this tutorial explains the same steps in more depth. {% hint style="info" %} Hand-editing the JSON files is still possible and fully supported. See the [JSON Schema Reference](/reference/json-schema.md) if you need to script config generation or tweak a value the generator doesn't expose. Most teams should use the generator, though: it validates your inputs and always produces a schema-correct config. {% endhint %} ## Fill in the form The generator is organized into six tabs. Work through them using the information you collected in [step 1](/tutorial/01-gather-your-robot-information.md): 1. **Gyro**: select your gyro type (`pigeon2_can`, `canandgyro_can`, `navx3_can`, `systemcore_internal` for the IMU built into the SystemCore, or `custom` to supply your own in code), its CAN ID and CAN bus, which axis reports yaw, and whether it needs to be inverted. The SystemCore IMU is not on CAN, so the CAN fields disappear when you pick it. `navx3_can` cannot be used with YAGSL 2027 yet, because StudicaLib has no `2027_alpha7` build. 2. **Front Left**, **Front Right**, **Back Left**, **Back Right** (one tab each): for every module, set the drive motor type/ID, angle motor type/ID, absolute encoder type/ID (or channel, for an encoder on a SystemCore DIO or analog port), any needed inversions, and the module's location relative to the robot center. Thrifty Nova motor types (`nova_neo`, `nova_minion`, `nova_pulsar`, and so on) are in the motor list alongside TalonFX, TalonFXS, SparkMAX and SparkFlex. 3. **Properties**: shared physical properties (gearing defaults, current limits) and starting PIDF gains for the drive and angle motors. ### CAN bus fields Every **CAN Bus** field takes the same values, whichever vendor made the device: | CAN Bus value | Bus | | --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | | empty | `can_s0`, the SystemCore's first CAN bus | | `0` to `4` | `can_s0` to `can_s4`, so `1` is `can_s1` | | `5` to `24` | The Motioncore buses `can_d0` to `can_d19` | | a CANivore name | CTRE devices only (TalonFX, TalonFXS, CANcoder, Pigeon 2.0) | The generator flags a bus number that does not exist, and a name on a device that only accepts a bus number (REV, Thrifty and Redux devices in the form). {% hint style="warning" %} CTRE devices with an empty CAN bus are on `can_s0`, like every other vendor. In YAGSL releases before `2026.10.09` they landed on Phoenix 6's own SystemCore default, `can_s2`. If your CTRE devices are wired to `can_s2`, enter `2`. {% endhint %} You can leave absolute encoder offsets and final PIDF gains at their defaults for now. You'll measure and tune those in the next two steps. The important thing at this stage is getting hardware types, IDs, CAN buses and module locations correct. ## Download and unzip When you're done, click **Download Config**. You get `swerve-config.zip`, which has `swervedrive.json` and the `modules` folder at its top level. Create the folder `src/main/deploy/swerve/base` in your project and extract the zip's contents into it, so the layout looks like this: ``` src/main/deploy └── swerve └── base ├── swervedrive.json └── modules ├── frontleft.json ├── frontright.json ├── backleft.json ├── backright.json ├── physicalproperties.json ├── pidfproperties.json └── pidfproperties_sim.json ``` `pidfproperties_sim.json` starts as a copy of `pidfproperties.json`. YAGSL reads it in place of `pidfproperties.json` when the robot program runs in simulation, so you can tune simulation gains without touching the gains for your real robot. {% hint style="info" %} The folder name is up to you, as long as it matches the path you hand to `SwerveParser.parse(...)` in [step 5](/tutorial/05-deploy-and-drive.md). This tutorial uses `swerve/base` throughout. {% endhint %} {% hint style="success" %} If you already have a config directory from a different robot, zip up its `swervedrive.json` and `modules` folder and use **Upload Config** to load it back into the generator to review or edit it, instead of starting from scratch. **Print** gives you a paper copy of the whole configuration for bring-up. {% endhint %} {% hint style="info" %} Bringing a config forward from a release before `2026.10.09`? pages.content: # Tune PIDF gains Starting points and a tuning procedure for your drive and angle motor gains. {% hint style="warning" %} Swerve steering/angle/azimuth motors have PID wrapping enabled at the topmost and bottommost point (e.g. "front" and "back"). When tuning angle PID you may want to test with left or right translation so the module doesn't cross the wrap point. {% endhint %} ## The basic idea YAGSL reads PIDF values from [`pidfproperties.json`](/reference/json-schema/pidfproperties-json.md) in your module folder. Generate or edit it with [**config.yagsl.com**](https://config.yagsl.com). This has been hashed and boiled down to the simplest form like this before: * **P**: if you're not where you want to be, get there. * **I**: if you haven't been where you want to be for a long time, get there faster. * **D**: if you're getting close to where you want to be, slow down. * [Video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qKy98Cbcltw) found by 78, found by [this CD post](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/finally-i-understand-pid/450811) ## Tuning procedure Another good way to describe it, [from CTRE](https://pro.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/latest/docs/api-reference/device-specific/talonfx/closed-loop-requests.html): Manual tuning typically follows this process: 1. Set $$P$$, $$I$$, and $$D$$ to zero. 2. Increase $$P$$ until the output **starts** to **oscillate** **around** the setpoint. 3. Increase $$D$$ as much as possible **without** introducing **jittering** to the response. For the drive motor, also set the feedforward terms (`s`, `v`, `a`; see below) before fine-tuning `P`; a good feedforward means `P` only has to correct small errors. ## WPILib walkthrough WPILib has lots of great documentation on PID, so it's worth reading directly: {% embed url="" %} Basics of PID {% endembed %} {% embed url="" %} Tuning velocity, like the drive motors! {% endembed %} {% embed url="" %} Tuning position, like the steering/angle/azimuth motors! {% endembed %} ## The current `pidfproperties.json` shape {% hint style="info" %} The schema changed in YAGSL 2026.8.05; `f` and `iz` (integral zone) and the old `output` clamp are gone. Feedforward is now expressed as `s`/`v`/`a` (`kS`/`kV`/`kA`, matching WPILib's `SimpleMotorFeedforward`). See the [schema changes reference](/reference/schema-changes.md) if you're migrating an older config by hand. {% endhint %} ```json { "drive": { "p": 0.02, "i": 0, "d": 0, "s": 0, "v": 0, "a": 0 }, "angle": { "p": 0.01, "i": 0, "d": 0, "s": 0, "v": 0, "a": 0 } } ``` If you leave drive `v` (kV) at `0`, YAGSL auto-derives it from the drive motor's free speed and your gearing, so a reasonable feedforward exists even before you've tuned anything by hand. You can also add a `pidfproperties_sim.json` alongside it. YAGSL will load that one instead when running in simulation (`RobotBase.isSimulation()`), so you can use looser gains in sim without touching your competition robot's config. ## Starting points The right PIDF values vary per-robot, but these are reasonable starting points to iterate from, organized by motor controller type. {% tabs %} {% tab title="SparkMax / SparkFlex" %} ```json { "drive": { "p": 0.0020645, "i": 0, "d": 0, "s": 0, "v": 0, "a": 0 }, "angle": { "p": 0.01, "i": 0, "d": 0, "s": 0, "v": 0, "a": 0 } } ``` {% endtab %} {% tab title="TalonFX" %} When the drive motor `type` for every module is `talonfx_*` (or alike: `krakenx60`, `falcon500`) this is a reasonable starting point: ```json { "drive": { "p": 1, "i": 0, "d": 0, "s": 0, "v": 0, "a": 0 }, "angle": { "p": 50, "i": 0, "d": 0.32, "s": 0, "v": 0, "a": 0 } } ``` {% endtab %} {% endtabs %} Once you have a reasonable starting point, use [**config.yagsl.com**](https://config.yagsl.com) to regenerate `pidfproperties.json` with your updated numbers, or hand-edit the file directly. Both work, since the parser only cares about the final JSON. ## Live tuning You don't have to redeploy for every gain change. YAMS publishes the drive's gains and setpoints to NetworkTables, so you can change them from a dashboard (Elastic, AdvantageScope) while the robot runs. The **Tuning Guide** at [config.yagsl.com](https://config.yagsl.com) walks through the full process; these are the pieces it uses. Live tuning needs `TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH` on the drive and both drive-to-pose controllers. YAMS only publishes the tuning command when both controllers are configured, even if you only want to tune the modules: ```java var cfg = new SwerveDriveConfig() .withSubsystem(this) // withMechanism(this) on Commands v3 .withTranslationController(new PIDController(4, 0, 0)) .withRotationController(new PIDController(3, 0, 0)) .withTelemetry("swerve", new SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig(TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH)); ``` 1. **Start in simulation**, or with the robot on blocks. Tuning moves the robot. 2. **Enable Utility mode** (formerly Test) and make sure nothing else is commanding the drive. The Commands v2 example holds the drive with an idle command so the default drive command can't fight the tuning command: ```java RobotModeTriggers.utility().whileTrue(Commands.idle(swerve).withName("Live Tuning")); ``` 3. **Start the tuning command** YAMS publishes under `Mechanisms/swerve/tuning` (click it in your dashboard, or set its `running` entry to `true`). Values under `Tuning/swerve/` only take effect while it runs. 4. **Turn on one tuning mode** below and adjust its values. Only one mode drives at a time; if you enable more than one, auto-align wins over drive tuning, and drive tuning wins over azimuth tuning. 5. **Copy the gains you settle on back** into `pidfproperties.json` (module gains) or your `SwerveDriveConfig` (drive-to-pose controllers). Live values are not saved and are gone on the next code restart. `swerve` in these paths is the telemetry name from `withTelemetry("swerve", ...)`. [YAMS' live tuning page](https://yams.yassrobotics.com/documentation/understanding/live-tuning#swerve-drive) walks through each swerve tuning mode step by step. | Key (under `Tuning/swerve/`) | What it does | Unit you type | | ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | | `modules/drive/enabled` | Drive tuning: drive every module at `modules/drive/velocity` | boolean | | `modules/drive/velocity` | Drive velocity setpoint | meters per second | | `modules/drive/inplace` | Point the modules tangent to the robot, so a positive velocity spins it in place (counter-clockwise) instead of driving straight | boolean | | `modules/drive/feedback/p`, `/i`, `/d` | Drive motor PID (`drive.p`/`i`/`d` in `pidfproperties.json`) | same as the JSON | | `modules/drive/feedforward/s`, `/v`, `/a` | Drive motor feedforward (`drive.s`/`v`/`a`) | same as the JSON | | `modules/azimuth/enabled` | Azimuth tuning: point every module at `modules/azimuth/angle` | boolean | | `modules/azimuth/angle` | Azimuth angle setpoint | degrees | | `modules/azimuth/feedback/p`, `/i`, `/d` | Azimuth motor PID (`angle.p`/`i`/`d`) | same as the JSON | | `modules/azimuth/feedforward/s`, `/v`, `/a` | Azimuth motor feedforward (`angle.s`/`v`/`a`) | same as the JSON | | `autoalign/enabled` | Auto-align tuning: drive to `autoalign/setpoint/*` with the drive-to-pose controllers | boolean | | `autoalign/setpoint/x`, `/y`, `/rot` | Auto-align target pose (field relative, blue origin) | meters, meters, degrees | | `autoalign/translation/p`, `/i`, `/d` | Translation controller (see [drive to a pose](/how-to-guides/drive-to-a-pose.md)) | per meter of error | | `autoalign/rotation/p`, `/i`, `/d` | Rotation controller | per radian of error | {% hint style="warning" %} **The units you type are not the units you read back.** YAMS' tunable fields use the units people think in: **degrees** and **RPM** for rotating mechanisms, **meters** and **meters per second** for linear ones (a swerve drive wheel is linear, so its velocity setpoint is in m/s). The read-only telemetry it publishes next to them, under `Mechanisms/swerve/...`, is in **rotations** and **rotations per second** (meters and m/s for linear measurements). So an azimuth setpoint of `90` (degrees) shows up as a `mechanism/position` of `0.25` (rotations). Check which table you're looking at before deciding a loop is "off by 360." {% endhint %} | Quantity | Tunable (under `Tuning/`) | Read-only telemetry (under `Mechanisms/`) | | ------------------------------ | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | | Angular position | degrees | rotations | | Angular velocity | RPM | rotations per second | | Linear position | meters | meters | | Linear velocity | meters per second | meters per second | | Gyro heading, absolute encoder | n/a | degrees | {% hint style="info" %} The example README lists one known issue for this release: dashboard auto-align only drives correctly while the robot faces 0° (away from the blue driver station). Zero the gyro facing 0° before enabling `autoalign/enabled`. The `driveToPose` commands themselves are not affected. {% endhint %} --- # Agent Instructions This documentation is published with GitBook. pages.title: Determine inversion
pages.content: # Determine inversion Work out which motors, encoders, and the gyro need to be inverted. Swerve modules and swerve drives require some inversions to get working properly. The goal is to get everything to increase **counter-clockwise positive (CCW+)**. {% hint style="info" %} [config.yagsl.com/guide](https://config.yagsl.com/guide) walks through this exact process interactively, with animations, if you'd rather follow along there instead of on this page. {% endhint %} {% hint style="warning" %} If your gears are grinding on the ground but not while on blocks, and your wheels are facing and spinning in the right directions, you may need to [tune PID](/how-to-guides/tune-pidf-gains.md) instead of inverting anything. {% endhint %} {% hint style="warning" %} If you invert incorrectly, your modules or robot may spin "out of control." If nothing here resolves it, see [The 8 steps](/how-to-guides/the-8-steps.md). {% endhint %} All of the telemetry referenced below lives under `Mechanisms/swerve` in NetworkTables. See [Telemetry, Simulation & Vision](/explanation/telemetry-and-vision.md) for the full tree. ## 1. Confirm the absolute encoder reads CCW+ With the robot lifted or on its side so the wheels spin freely, rotate one module by hand **counterclockwise** (viewed from directly above, robot front pointing away from you) and watch that module's `modules//encoder` value in AdvantageScope. * If it **increases**, the absolute encoder is already correct; leave `absoluteEncoderInverted` as `false`. * If it **decreases**, set `absoluteEncoderInverted` to `true` for that module. This is rare because most absolute encoders already read CCW+ by default. ```json { "drive": { "type": "sparkmax_neo", "id": 2, "canbus": "" }, "angle": { "type": "sparkmax_neo", "id": 1, "canbus": "" }, "absoluteEncoder": { "type": "cancoder_can", "id": 10, "channel": 0, "canbus": "" }, "inverted": { "drive": false, "angle": false }, "absoluteEncoderInverted": true, "absoluteEncoderOffset": -50.977, "location": { "front": 12, "left": -12 } } ``` Once every module reads CCW+, rotate each wheel to point straight forward (bevel gear left) and record the `modules//encoder` value held in that position. That's the module's `absoluteEncoderOffset`. Enter it in the module's JSON, or paste it into [**config.yagsl.com**](https://config.yagsl.com). ## 2. Confirm the gyro reads CCW+ With the robot lifted off the ground, rotate the **entire robot** counterclockwise (viewed from above) and watch `Mechanisms/swerve/gyro`. * If it **increases**, leave `gyroInvert` alone; there's nothing to change. * If it **decreases**, set `gyroInvert` to `true` in `swervedrive.json`: ```json { "gyro": { "type": "pigeon2_can", "id": 13, "canbus": "canivore" }, "gyroAxis": "yaw", "gyroInvert": true, "modules": ["frontleft.json", "frontright.json", "backleft.json", "backright.json"] } ``` See the [gyroscope reference](/reference/hardware/gyroscopes.md) for the full list of supported `gyro.type` values. {% hint style="info" %} If the gyro is mounted on its side, so that turning the robot shows up as the sensor's roll or pitch, set `gyroAxis` to `roll` or `pitch` first and then run this check. `gyroInvert` is applied to the heading after the axis is chosen. Both are ignored for a [`custom` gyro](/how-to-guides/use-a-custom-gyro.md), which sets them in Java instead. {% endhint %} {% hint style="warning" %} Re-run this check after updating to YAGSL 2027, especially with a Redux Canandgyro. Older releases inverted a Canandgyro's heading twice; inversion is now applied exactly once, by `gyroInvert`, so a config that compensated for the old behavior needs `gyroInvert` flipped. {% endhint %} ## 3. Spin test: catch drive motor inversion and module swaps Still with the robot lifted off the ground, deploy code and drive with a joystick input that commands pure rotation (e.g. hold the rotation stick fully to one side). Watch the robot against AdvantageScope's Swerve widget (top-down view; see [Set up AdvantageScope](/how-to-guides/set-up-advantagescope.md)) and compare: | Symptom | Likely cause | | --------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Modules drift or translate instead of spinning cleanly in place | Wrong CAN IDs for a module, or a wrong `absoluteEncoderOffset`. | | Spins cleanly, but the wrong way (clockwise instead of CCW) | Inverted drive motor(s); a diagonal module swap (front-left ↔ back-right, front-right ↔ back-left); or an absolute encoder offset captured with the bevel gear facing right instead of left. | If a single module is spinning the wrong way, invert that module's drive motor: ```json { "drive": { "type": "sparkmax_neo", "id": 2, "canbus": "" }, "angle": { "type": "sparkmax_neo", "id": 1, "canbus": "" }, "absoluteEncoder": { "type": "cancoder_can", "id": 10, "channel": 0, "canbus": "" }, "inverted": { "drive": true, "angle": false }, "absoluteEncoderInverted": false, "absoluteEncoderOffset": -50.977, "location": { "front": 12, "left": -12 } } ``` If every module spins the wrong way at once, double-check for a diagonal module swap in `swervedrive.json`'s `modules` list before you start flipping individual `inverted.drive` fields. It's a more common cause than it sounds. ## 4. Field-orientation check Once the spin test looks right, put the robot down and drive it forward/back/left/right at its starting heading while watching a 2D/3D Field tab fed from `Mechanisms/swerve/pose`. Then spin in place again, this time watching the field widget's heading instead of the swerve module widget. * **Wrong at every heading, including the start:** check `gyroInvert`. * **Only wrong once you rotate away from the starting heading:** an absolute encoder offset that's off, a drive motor inversion mistake, a wrong module `location`, an absolute encoder wired to the wrong motor controller, or a wrong CAN ID. Verify wiring and CAN IDs first because they're the fastest to rule out. * **The spin test in step 3 looked right, but the field widget's heading spins backwards:** an inverted gyro can flip the field widget even when the module states widget looked correct. {% hint style="danger" %} #### Odometry mismatch If your robot drives backwards in odometry but forwards in real life, while a spin-in-place still shows Counter-Clockwise-Positive movement, apply this patch: add `180` to every `absoluteEncoderOffset` in every module file. {% endhint %} {% hint style="info" %} In older YAGSL configs (pre-2026.8.05) this section was named `imu`/`invertedIMU` instead of `gyro`/`gyroInvert`. See the [schema changes reference](/reference/schema-changes.md) if you're working from an old config. {% endhint %} --- # Agent Instructions This documentation is published with GitBook. pages.title: Put devices on a different CAN bus
pages.content: # Put devices on a different CAN bus Tell YAGSL which SystemCore, Motioncore or vendor CAN bus each device is on with the canbus field. The SystemCore has several CAN buses instead of one, so every CAN device in your YAGSL JSON (drive and angle motors, absolute encoders, the gyro) has a `canbus` field saying which bus it is wired to. YAGSL reads that field the same way for every vendor. {% hint style="warning" %} **Behavior change for CTRE devices.** An empty `canbus` now always means SystemCore bus `can_s0`, for every vendor. Before, CTRE devices with an empty `canbus` ended up on Phoenix 6's own SystemCore default, `can_s2`. If your TalonFX, CANcoder or Pigeon 2 devices are wired to `can_s2`, they now need `"canbus": "2"`. {% endhint %} ## 1. Find the bus each device is wired to | `canbus` value | Bus | | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | | `""` (or left out) | SystemCore `can_s0` | | `"0"` to `"4"` | SystemCore `can_s0` to `can_s4` | | `"5"` to `"24"` | Motioncore `can_d0` to `can_d19` | | Any other text | Passed to the vendor as is, for example a CANivore's name for CTRE | So a device on `can_s1` gets `"canbus": "1"`, and the first Motioncore bus, `can_d0`, is `"5"`. A number outside 0 to 24 stops the robot program at startup with `CAN bus does not exist`. ## 2. Set `canbus` on each device `canbus` is a string, so bus numbers are quoted: ```json { "drive": { "type": "sparkflex_vortex", "id": 2, "canbus": "1" }, "angle": { "type": "sparkmax_neo550", "id": 1, "canbus": "1" }, "absoluteEncoder": { "type": "cancoder_can", "id": 10, "channel": 0, "canbus": "" }, "inverted": { "drive": false, "angle": false }, "absoluteEncoderOffset": -50.977, "location": { "front": 12, "left": 12 } } ``` ```json { "gyro": { "type": "pigeon2_can", "id": 13, "canbus": "canivore" }, "gyroAxis": "yaw", "gyroInvert": false, "modules": ["frontleft.json", "frontright.json", "backleft.json", "backright.json"] } ``` Devices in one module don't have to share a bus, and neither do the modules. ## 3. Check what your vendor accepts Not every vendor can use a bus name: | Vendor | Accepted `canbus` values | | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | CTRE (`talonfx_*`, `talonfxs_*`, `cancoder_can`, `pigeon2_can`) | Empty, a bus number, or a CANivore's name or serial number | | REV (`sparkmax_*`, `sparkflex_*`, `splineencoder_can`) | Empty or a bus number only | | Thrifty (`nova_*`) | Empty or a bus number only | | Redux (`canandgyro_can`, `canandmag_can`) | Empty, a bus number, or a ReduxLib bus string such as `socketcan:can_s1` | | Studica (`navx3_can`), AndyMark (`andymarkhexbore_can`) | `canbus` is not used; the device is created from its CAN ID alone. Neither device works with YAGSL 2027 yet, because their vendor libraries have no `2027_alpha7` build | That includes port names: a SPARK on `can_s1` is `"1"`, not `"CAN_S1"`. Giving a REV or Thrifty device anything other than a bus number stops the robot program at startup with an `IllegalArgumentException` like: ``` REV devices only use the Systemcore and Motioncore CAN buses, but canbus is "canivore". Use "" for can_s0, or the bus number, such as "1" for can_s1. ``` Encoders with an `_attached`, `_dio` or `_analog` type are not on CAN at all, so their `canbus` is ignored. An `_attached` encoder is read through the angle motor controller, on that controller's bus. ## 4. Verify it Deploy and check the Driver Station console. A wrong bus doesn't stop the program the way a malformed value does: the device is simply never found, so you get that vendor's usual "device not detected" alerts and a module that doesn't respond. If one module or one vendor's devices are missing, compare its `canbus` against the bus it is physically wired to before looking anywhere else. --- # Agent Instructions This documentation is published with GitBook. pages.title: The 8 steps
pages.content:
# The 8 steps ## Something is wrong but it's driving-ish? When changing inversion states doesn't work and nothing else you know of fixes the issue, debugging can be painful and arduous. Here are the eight steps that are unfortunately necessary to work through it. Affectionately known as *"Translational Axis change based off of the robot heading"* (the X and Y axis change in field-oriented control based on your robot turning), these steps will resolve it somewhere along the way. ## Prepare your robot code To run these tests, use the following (or a variation of it) as your drive code. You may need to port it to your joystick or negate axis data. {% code title="RobotContainer.java" %} ```java SwerveDriveSubsystem swerve; CommandXboxController driverXbox; // Xbox sticks read negative when pushed forward/left, while robot controls are // front-left positive, so every axis is negated. // Left stick controls translation, right stick points the desired // heading directly (NOT angular velocity). SwerveInputStream driveDirectAngle = swerve.getAngularVelocityStream(() -> -driverXbox.getLeftY(), () -> -driverXbox.getLeftX(), () -> -driverXbox.getRightX()) .withControllerHeadingAxis(() -> -driverXbox.getRightX(), () -> -driverXbox.getRightY()) .withHeadingControl(() -> true) .withDeadband(0.05) .withAllianceRelativeControl(); swerve.setDefaultCommand(swerve.driveFieldRelative(driveDirectAngle)); ``` {% endcode %} `getAngularVelocityStream(x, y, rot)` and `driveFieldRelative(stream)` are the two small helpers from the YAGSL `commands2` example's `SwerveDriveSubsystem`: the first returns `SwerveInputStream.of(drive, x, y, rot)` and the second runs `drive.setFieldRelativeChassisSpeeds(stream.get())` every loop. On Commands v3, use the `commands3` example's `HeadingTeleop` opmode, which builds the same stream and drives it from a `while (true)` coroutine. `withControllerHeadingAxis(headingX, headingY)` plus `withHeadingControl(() -> true)` makes the robot turn to face wherever the right stick points instead of spinning at an angular velocity, the same "point the stick where you want the robot to face" behavior the old `SwerveController.getTargetSpeeds()` heading-hold path provided. Heading control needs a rotation controller on the drive (`SwerveDriveConfig.withRotationController(...)`). If you leave `withHeadingControl` off and drive with the angular-velocity stream instead, the steps below are identical; only the exact symptom description changes slightly. {% hint style="info" %} A stick heading is field relative, not alliance relative. If you're testing from the red alliance wall, flip both heading axes (multiply them by `-1`), as the `commands2` example's `RobotContainer` does. {% endhint %} ## The eight steps {% hint style="danger" %} **The steps are dangerous.** Six of them will cause your robot to spin out of control. One of them will be correct. One of them will appear to be correct but have the translational axis change based on the robot's heading. {% endhint %} {% hint style="warning" %} You are not expected to complete all of these steps to get a functioning swerve drive. Somewhere along the way your issue should disappear. {% endhint %} 1. Start by setting `gyroInvert` in `swervedrive.json` to `false` **AND** `inverted.drive` to `false` in every module JSON. 2. THEN set `gyroInvert` to `true`. 3. THEN invert all of the drive motors in the module JSONs by setting `inverted.drive` to `true`. 4. THEN set `gyroInvert` back to `false`. 5. THEN [flip the modules](#user-content-fn-1)[^1].\\ 6. THEN un-invert all of the drive motors (`inverted.drive` back to `false`). 7. THEN set `gyroInvert` to `true`. 8. THEN set your drive motors' `inverted.drive` back to `true`. {% hint style="danger" %} IF none of these work, you most likely have an incorrect hardware configuration, something is not working as expected, or something is wired incorrectly. {% endhint %} ## Verifying behavior Sometimes the eight steps don't look done when they really are. Here's an example where the robot is actually tuned correctly, but the desired front of the robot is really the back of the robot.
How to swap module configurations For the examples, we label modules with numbers to reduce confusion; when changing module files around, we assign the numbers to the respective initial module configuration names. For the example above: 1. `frontleft.json` 2. `frontright.json` 3. `backleft.json` 4. `backright.json` **Swapping `frontleft.json` with `backright.json`** ```json { "drive": { "type": "sparkmax_neo", "id": 4, "canbus": "" }, "angle": { "type": "sparkmax_neo", "id": 3, "canbus": "" }, "absoluteEncoder": { "type": "cancoder_can", "id": 9, "channel": 0, "canbus": "" }, "inverted": { "drive": false, "angle": false }, "absoluteEncoderOffset": -114.609, "location": { "front": 12, "left": 12 } } ``` ```json { "drive": { "type": "sparkmax_neo", "id": 5, "canbus": "" }, "angle": { "type": "sparkmax_neo", "id": 6, "canbus": "" }, "absoluteEncoder": { "type": "cancoder_can", "id": 11, "channel": 0, "canbus": "" }, "inverted": { "drive": false, "angle": false }, "absoluteEncoderOffset": -18.281, "location": { "front": -12, "left": -12 } } ``` Swap the device IDs and offsets between the two files (keep each file's own `location`) and you've swapped the module configurations correctly. #### The easy way 1. Change the `location` negations to the desired module side. 2. Rename the files without overwriting each other.
[^1]: Change the device configuration for the drive AND angle motor controllers AND the absolute encoders in the following way: (Front Left -> Back Right) (Front Right -> Back Left) (Back Left -> Front Right) (Back Right -> Front Left) --- # Agent Instructions This documentation is published with GitBook. pages.title: Fix common SparkMAX/SparkFlex problems
pages.content:
# Fix common SparkMAX/SparkFlex problems

These usually show up on MAXSwerve robots.

## NEOs can damage SparkMAX controllers

When a NEO heats up enough from being stalled too long, it will short positive to the sensor cable, sending very high current through the low-current sensor channel and melting the SparkMax PCB. This WILL kill your SparkMAX, and every SparkMAX plugged into your killer NEO.

This can also kill your laptop if you plug into a powered-on SparkMAX, because the short can extend to the USB port.

{% embed url="<https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1uM_uPD5HjzGwYUOmzZOmmgb1-KANiTTKI3o9aIJlPcc/edit?slide=id.p#slide=id.p>" %}

## SparkMAX absolute encoder boards

The [SparkMAX Absolute Encoder board](https://www.revrobotics.com/rev-11-3326/) should be zip-tied and hot-glued to the SparkMAX for redundancy and to prevent it from coming loose.

### Throughbore connection to the absolute encoder board

The connector between the [SparkMax Absolute Encoder board](https://www.revrobotics.com/rev-11-3326/) and the [REV Throughbore](https://www.revrobotics.com/rev-11-1271/) should be hot-glued down on **BOTH** connection points, because these can come loose.

The wire should also be tensioned just right. If it's over-tensioned, the wire might not be fully seated in the connector, and the data could be incomplete, corrupted, or unavailable.

## Absolute encoder attached via the SparkMax's duty-cycle port

When you use an absolute encoder wired to the SparkMax through its Absolute Encoder board, give it an `_attached` type in the module JSON, such as `revthroughbore_attached` (see the [absolute encoder reference](/reference/hardware/absolute-encoders.md) for the exact type string for your device). YAGSL then reads it through the angle motor's SparkMax instead of creating a separate device, so `id` and `channel` are not used.

```json
{
  "absoluteEncoder": { "type": "revthroughbore_attached", "id": 1, "channel": 0, "canbus": "" }
}
```

{% hint style="success" %}
When the absolute encoder is attached to the azimuth motor controller (e.g. a REV Throughbore wired into a SparkMax), YAGSL automatically wires it up as the SparkMax's closed-loop feedback sensor and applies `absoluteEncoderOffset` as its zero offset for you. There is no manual "set the `factor` to `360`" workaround to remember, and no `useExternalFeedbackSensor()`/`useInternalFeedbackSensor()` calls to make in your own code. Just set `absoluteEncoderOffset` in the module JSON (or via [**config.yagsl.com**](https://config.yagsl.com)) and the parser handles the rest.
{% endhint %}

{% hint style="info" %}
If you're migrating an old config that hand-set `physicalproperties.json`'s `factor` to `360` as a workaround, that field no longer exists. See the [schema changes reference](/reference/schema-changes.md).
{% endhint %}

## SPARK devices not found after moving to the SystemCore

Two things changed for REV hardware in YAGSL 2027:

* **REVLib is no longer pulled in by the YAGSL vendordep.** YAGSL only requires YAMS and loads REVLib by reflection when your JSON uses a `sparkmax_*`/`sparkflex_*` device, so install the REVLib vendordep yourself or the parser fails at startup when it tries to build the first SPARK.
* **`canbus` must be empty or a bus number.** `""` is SystemCore bus `can_s0`, `"1"` is `can_s1`, and so on. A name (such as a CANivore's) is rejected with an `IllegalArgumentException` saying REV devices only use the SystemCore and Motioncore CAN buses. See [How to put devices on a different CAN bus](/how-to-guides/choose-a-can-bus.md).

## Status frame error

Usually, a status frame error means your connection to the REV Throughbore is incomplete somehow, or the sensor cable from your motor is loose or broken.

If you see this, check **ALL SENSOR CABLES GOING INTO THAT SPARKMAX**.

pages.content: # Set up AdvantageScope AdvantageScope is a data visualization tool, courtesy of team 6328 Mechanical Advantage, which can visualize the swerve drive to give you feedback for debugging. ## Opening Since the 2024 season, [AdvantageScope](https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/AdvantageScope) has been included with the WPILib installation. There is no external download required, but with every WPILib update you should re-download the [WPILib installer](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/zero-to-robot/step-2/wpilib-setup.html) to get the latest version of WPILib tools. ## Configuring AdvantageScope 1. Connect your laptop to the robot. 2. Open `AdvantageScope (WPILib)`, or in VS Code open the command palette and type `WPILib: Start Tool`, then click `AdvantageScope`. 3. Click `Help`, then `Show Preferences`. 4. In the **Robot Address** field, enter the SystemCore's IP address based on your team number: `10.TE.AM.2`. 5. Connect to the robot (or the simulator). 6. On the right side of the window, click `+` to add a new tab. 7. Add a new 🦀 Swerve tab. 8. In the Sources field, drag in each `Mechanisms/swerve` field: * `Mechanisms/swerve/states/current` * `Mechanisms/swerve/states/desired` * `Mechanisms/swerve/chassis/current` * `Mechanisms/swerve/chassis/desired` {% hint style="info" %} You may need to enable your robot before AdvantageScope shows values for these fields. {% endhint %} {% hint style="info" %} `swerve` is the telemetry name you gave the drive with `SwerveDriveConfig.withTelemetry("swerve", ...)`; if you named it something else, look under `Mechanisms/`. The `current` fields need `TelemetryVerbosity.MID` or higher and the `desired` fields need `TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH`. {% endhint %} To see the robot's pose on a 2D/3D field, add a **2D Field** or **3D Field** tab instead and drag in `Mechanisms/swerve/pose`. ## Reading the display {% hint style="info" %} The **RED** lines are the measured velocity and position of each swerve module. The **BLUE** lines are the velocity and position each module was commanded to. {% endhint %} Large, persistent gaps between the red and blue lines usually point to a tuning issue. pages.title: View your DataLog in AdvantageScope
pages.content: # View your DataLog in AdvantageScope Pull the .wpilog off your robot and look at what actually happened during a match or test run. {% hint style="danger" %} **This is not "Log Replay."** [AdvantageKit's Log Replay](https://docs.advantagekit.org/getting-started/what-is-advantagekit) re-runs your robot code against a recorded log to deterministically reproduce a match in simulation, and requires the AdvantageKit IO-interface pattern. What this page covers is simpler and works with **every** YAGSL robot, AdvantageKit or not: opening the `.wpilog` file your robot already wrote and looking at the recorded values in AdvantageScope. Nothing re-executes; you're just viewing a file. {% endhint %} YAGSL's swerve telemetry can be written to a WPILib `DataLog` as well as published to NetworkTables. See [Telemetry, Simulation & Vision](/explanation/telemetry-and-vision.md) for the live NetworkTables tree; this page is the practical walkthrough for looking at a *recorded* run afterward. ## Step 1: Make sure a DataLog is actually being written `DataLogManager` owns the actual file on disk. Start it once, early, in your `Robot` constructor (WPILib 2027 has no `robotInit()`): ```java import org.wpilib.driverstation.DriverStation; import org.wpilib.system.DataLogManager; public Robot() { DataLogManager.start(); DriverStation.startDataLog(DataLogManager.getLog()); // optional: also logs joystick/DS data } ``` {% hint style="info" %} If you never call `DataLogManager.start()` yourself, it still starts lazily the first time YAMS creates a DataLog entry. Calling it explicitly, before you build the swerve drive, guarantees the log begins at power-on and lets you fold in DS/joystick data with `DriverStation.startDataLog(...)`. {% endhint %} On the real robot, `.wpilog` files are written to a `logs` folder on a USB drive if one is plugged in (`/u/logs`), otherwise to `/home/systemcore/logs` on the SystemCore's internal storage. In simulation, they land in your project's `logs/` folder next to `build.gradle`. WPILib initially names the file `WPILIB_TBD_.wpilog` and renames it to a UTC timestamp (e.g. `WPILIB_20261009_010558.wpilog`) once the Driver Station connects, or to `WPILIB___.wpilog` when the FMS provides a match number. {% hint style="warning" %} `WPILIB_TBD_*` files left over from a previous boot are deleted on startup, and the oldest logs are deleted when the storage has less than 50 MB free. Pull the logs you care about off the robot. {% endhint %} ## Step 2: Give the swerve drive a DataLog name By default `DataLogManager` records every NetworkTables value change, so everything under `Mechanisms/swerve` is already in the file (as `NT:/Mechanisms/swerve/...`) without any setup. To also get YAMS' dedicated DataLog entries, which keep recording when you turn NetworkTables publishing off for competition, name them on the telemetry config you pass to `SwerveDriveConfig`: ```java import yams.core.telemetry.SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig; import yams.core.telemetry.enums.TelemetryVerbosity; var cfg = new SwerveDriveConfig() .withSubsystem(this) // withMechanism(this) on Commands v3 .withTelemetry("swerve", new SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig(TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH) .withDataLogName("Swerve")); ``` `SwerveParser` then derives a DataLog name for every module and motor from that one name: * `Swerve`: the drive itself (pose, gyro, chassis speeds, module states). * `Swerve/modules/`: that module's absolute encoder and state. * `Swerve/modules//drive`: that module's drive motor. * `Swerve/modules//azimuth`: that module's angle/steering motor. Numeric entries have their unit inserted after that prefix, for example `Swerve/degrees/gyro`, `Swerve/modules/frontleft/degrees/encoder`, or `Swerve/modules/frontleft/azimuth/rotations/mechanism/position`. Struct entries such as `Swerve/pose` and `Swerve/states/current` do not. Tunable (live tuning) fields are never written to the DataLog. {% hint style="info" %} If you use the shorter `withTelemetry("swerve", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH)` overload instead, `SwerveParser` names the drive's DataLog `Swerve` for you, but only the drive-level entries are created, not the per-module or per-motor ones. Pass a `SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig` with `withDataLogName(...)` as above to get all of them. A `SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig` without a DataLog name creates no dedicated entries at all (the `NT:` mirror is still recorded). {% endhint %} {% hint style="warning" %} Note the DataLog tree uses a top-level `Swerve` (the name you chose, no `Mechanisms` prefix), a *different* root than the live NetworkTables tree covered in [Telemetry, Simulation & Vision](/explanation/telemetry-and-vision.md) (`Mechanisms/swerve`, from the telemetry name). Both describe the same data; AdvantageScope shows them as two separate branches in the field tree (`Swerve` for the DataLog-only entries, `NT` for the mirrored NetworkTables ones). See the sidebar in the screenshots below. {% endhint %} Which fields exist depends on the `TelemetryVerbosity`: `LOW` logs the pose and gyro, `MID` adds the measured chassis speeds and module states, and `HIGH` adds the desired ones. ## Step 3: Run it and record Deploy or simulate the robot, enable it, and drive around for a bit. Every field above writes to both NetworkTables and the DataLog on each `drive.updateTelemetry()` call. ## Step 4: Pull the file and open it in AdvantageScope 1. Grab the `.wpilog` off the SystemCore (the USB drive, or `scp systemcore@10.TE.AM.2:/home/systemcore/logs/*.wpilog .`), or straight from your sim project's `logs/` folder. 2. Open **AdvantageScope**, then **File → Open File...** (or drag the `.wpilog` onto the window). Do **not** use "Connect to Robot/Simulator". That connects live over NetworkTables, which shows *current* values, not the recorded run. ## Step 5: Explore the data Add a tab to visualize the data: * **2D Field** tab: drag `Swerve/pose` in to see the robot's recorded path. * **Swerve** tab: AdvantageScope's built-in module visualizer. Drag `Swerve/states/current` (and optionally `Swerve/states/desired` and `Swerve/chassis/current`/`desired`) into the **Sources** list to see wheel vectors animate over the timeline. * **Line Graph** tab: drag any numeric field to plot it over time. A useful pairing while debugging: each module's `Swerve/modules//azimuth/rotations/mechanism/position` (the angle motor's own position, in rotations) against `Swerve/modules//degrees/encoder` (the absolute encoder, in degrees; also in the file as `NT:/Mechanisms/swerve/modules//encoder`). If the two drift apart over a run, once you account for the units, the angle motor's encoder was seeded from the wrong absolute offset. pages.title: JSON Configuration Schema
pages.content:
# JSON Configuration Schema

YAGSL builds a YAMS `SwerveDrive` from a directory of JSON files. `SwerveParser` (`swervelib.commands2.SwerveParser` or `swervelib.commands3.SwerveParser`, both built on `swervelib.core.parser.SwerveParser`) reads this directory and constructs the equivalent YAMS `SwerveDriveConfig` / `SwerveModuleConfig` / `SmartMotorControllerConfig` objects for you. You rarely need to hand-edit these files, since [config.yagsl.com](https://config.yagsl.com) generates them for you, but knowing the schema is useful for debugging, scripting, or hand-tweaking a single value.

{% hint style="info" %}
If you're setting up a robot for the first time, use the [Tutorial](/tutorial/tutorial.md) section instead. This is reference material for looking up exact field names and types.
{% endhint %}

## Directory layout

```
src/main/deploy
└── swerve
    └── base                       <- name is arbitrary, passed to `SwerveParser.parse(...)`
        ├── swervedrive.json
        └── modules
            ├── frontleft.json
            ├── frontright.json
            ├── backleft.json
            ├── backright.json     <- module filenames are arbitrary, referenced by swervedrive.json
            ├── physicalproperties.json
            ├── pidfproperties.json
            └── pidfproperties_sim.json   (optional)
```

`SwerveParser.parse(directory)` reads, in order:

1. `swervedrive.json`: top-level drive config, the gyro plus the list of module files.
2. `modules/pidfproperties.json`: default PID + feedforward gains shared by every module. If `modules/pidfproperties_sim.json` also exists, it's used instead whenever `RobotBase.isSimulation()` is `true`, so you can tune sim and real gains independently.
3. `modules/physicalproperties.json`: default gearing and current limits shared by every module.
4. Each file listed in `swervedrive.json`'s `modules` array: one per swerve module, describing that module's hardware, wiring, and location. A module file may override the gearing from `physicalproperties.json` with its own `gearing` object.

The JSON is read with WPILib's JSON library (avaje-jsonb), using adapters generated at compile time for the classes in `swervelib.core.parser.json`. Fields a class doesn't have (for example a `$schema` key, or a field left over from an older config) are ignored rather than rejected, and fields missing from a file keep the default listed on each page.

{% hint style="warning" %}
Device `type` strings are **not** checked while the files are read. An invalid or unsupported `type` only fails later, when `SwerveParser.createSwerveDrive(...)` builds that device.
{% endhint %}

## Pages in this section

* [swervedrive.json](/reference/json-schema/swervedrive-json.md)
* [module json (per-module file)](/reference/json-schema/module-json.md)
* [physicalproperties.json](/reference/json-schema/physicalproperties-json.md)
* [pidfproperties.json / pidfproperties\_sim.json](/reference/json-schema/pidfproperties-json.md)
* [Device type strings](/reference/json-schema/device-types.md): every valid `type` value for gyros, motor controllers, and absolute encoders.

{% hint style="warning" %}
Moving a 2026 config to YAGSL 2027, or coming from a pre-2026.8.05 `swerve/` directory (`imu`, `encoder`, `conversionFactors`, `controllerproperties.json`, PIDF `f`/`iz`)? See [Schema Changes](/reference/schema-changes.md) for both migration guides.
{% endhint %}

## Control system and CAN buses

YAGSL 2027 runs on the SystemCore, which has several CAN buses of its own (`can_s0` to `can_s4`) and more on an attached Motioncore (`can_d0` to `can_d19`). Every device's `canbus` field is read the same way for every vendor, by `swervelib.core.parser.CANBuses`:

| `canbus` value          | CAN bus                                                                |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `""` (empty or missing) | SystemCore `can_s0`                                                    |
| `"0"` to `"4"`          | SystemCore `can_s0` to `can_s4`, so `"1"` is `can_s1`                  |
| `"5"` to `"24"`         | Motioncore `can_d0` to `can_d19`, so `"5"` is `can_d0`                 |
| any other number        | Rejected with `CAN bus <n> does not exist`                             |
| anything else           | Passed to the vendor as is, such as a CANivore's name for CTRE devices |

The bus numbers follow WPILib's `CANPort` enum. Whitespace around the value is trimmed, and `canbus` is always a JSON **string** (`"1"`, not `1`). For a step by step guide, see [Put devices on a different CAN bus](/how-to-guides/choose-a-can-bus.md).

What each vendor does with a value that is not a bus number:

| Vendor                                                          | Non-numeric `canbus`                                                             |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| CTRE (`talonfx_*`, `talonfxs_*`, `pigeon2_can`, `cancoder_can`) | Used as the Phoenix 6 `CANBus` name, such as a CANivore's name or serial number. |
| Redux (`canandgyro_can`, `canandmag_can`)                       | Used as a ReduxLib bus string, such as `"socketcan:can_s1"`.                     |
| REV (`sparkmax_*`, `sparkflex_*`, `splineencoder_can`)          | Rejected. REV devices only accept `""` or a bus number.                          |
| ThriftyBot (`nova_*`)                                           | Rejected. Thrifty devices only accept `""` or a bus number.                      |

`canbus` is ignored for devices that aren't on CAN (`systemcore_internal`, `custom`, and `_dio`, `_analog`, and `_attached` absolute encoders). It is currently also ignored by `navx3_can` and `andymarkhexbore_can`, which are always created on their vendor library's default bus.

{% hint style="warning" %}
**Changed in 2027:** a CTRE device with an empty `canbus` is now on `can_s0`, like every other vendor. Before the `canbus` values were unified in `2026.10.09` it ended up on `can_s2`, so a CTRE device wired to `can_s2` now needs `"canbus": "2"`. REV devices no longer accept a port name such as `"can_s1"`; use the bus number `"1"`.
{% endhint %}

pages.title: swervedrive.json
pages.content:
# swervedrive.json

Top-level drive configuration. Parsed into `swervelib.core.parser.json.SwerveDriveJson`.

```json
{
  "gyro": {
    "type": "pigeon2_can",
    "id": 0,
    "canbus": ""
  },
  "gyroAxis": "yaw",
  "gyroInvert": false,
  "modules": ["frontleft.json", "frontright.json", "backleft.json", "backright.json"]
}
```

| Field        | Type                                                  | Required             | Description                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `gyro`       | [Device](/reference/json-schema/device-types.md#gyro) | yes                  | The robot's gyroscope. See [Device type strings](/reference/json-schema/device-types.md#gyro) for valid `type` values.                                                         |
| `gyroAxis`   | string enum                                           | no (default `"yaw"`) | Which axis of the gyro points up through the robot and is read as the heading: `yaw`, `pitch`, or `roll`. Passed to YAMS as `SwerveDriveConfig.withGyroHeadingAxis(GyroAxis)`. |
| `gyroInvert` | boolean                                               | yes                  | Invert the gyroscope's heading reading. Passed to YAMS as `SwerveDriveConfig.withGyroInverted(boolean)`; the parser does not invert the gyro itself.                           |
| `modules`    | string\[]                                             | yes                  | Filenames (relative to the `modules/` directory) of each module's JSON file, minimum 3, listed clockwise from front-left by convention.                                        |

## `gyro` object

| Field    | Type   | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| -------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `type`   | string | Gyro type string, see [Device type strings](/reference/json-schema/device-types.md#gyro). Set to `custom` to skip YAGSL's gyro setup and configure the gyro yourself; see [Custom Gyro](/reference/hardware/gyroscopes.md#custom-gyro).                                       |
| `id`     | number | CAN ID. Set to `0` if the gyro doesn't need one (`systemcore_internal`, `custom`).                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `canbus` | string | CAN bus the gyro is on: `""` for the SystemCore bus `can_s0`, or the bus number, such as `"1"` for `can_s1`. A Pigeon 2 also takes a CANivore's name. See [CAN buses](/reference/json-schema.md#control-system-and-can-buses). Ignored by `systemcore_internal` and `custom`. |

{% hint style="info" %}
When `gyro.type` is `custom`, `gyroAxis` and `gyroInvert` above are also ignored. The parser never calls `SwerveDriveConfig.withGyro()`/`withGyroHeadingAxis()`/`withGyroInverted()`, so you must call them yourself.
{% endhint %}
